evidence.claim: Designated a Washington State Scenic and Recreational Highway, it links Salmon La Sac with Ellensburg.
evidence.quote: The Swiftwater Corridor Scenic Byway is a Washington State Scenic and Recreational Highway in Kittitas County, Washington, United States. It follows five highways from the Salmon La Sac campground near Roslyn to Ellensburg:

evidence.claim: Scenic Washington presents a longer journey continuing to Vantage on the Columbia River, highlighting communities bypassed by faster traffic.
evidence.quote: This byway rambles through the back roads between Salmon La Sac near the Snoqualmie Pass summit and Vantage on the Columbia River and reveals natural beauty, signs of the past and country communities that travelers on the speedier bypass miss out on entirely.

evidence.claim: Highway travel changed these towns alongside the railroads and mines.
evidence.quote: In 1913, steps were taken to improve automobile access across the Cascade Mountains via Snoqualmie Pass.

evidence.claim: Highway travel changed these towns alongside the railroads and mines.
evidence.quote: The location of U.S. Route 10 (now State Route 10) north of Thorp in 1926, and the eventual opening of Interstate 90 in 1968, all played vital roles in the changing population and economic conditions that shaped the small community.

evidence.claim: In 1913, state highway funding supported construction of the Sunset Highway between Seattle and Spokane, with its route passing directly through Cle Elum’s business district.
evidence.quote: A $1,500,000 levy (equivalent to $48,900,000 in 2025) was approved in 1913 to improve and expand the state's highways. The largest project award from the levy ($590,743) went to construction of the Sunset Highway between Spokane and Seattle. This major cross-state highway would pass directly through Cle Elum's business district

evidence.claim: Farther east, US 10 ran north of Thorp in 1926; Interstate 90 opened in 1968.
evidence.quote: The location of U.S. Route 10 (now State Route 10) north of Thorp in 1926, and the eventual opening of Interstate 90 in 1968

evidence.claim: Roslyn’s 26 adjoining cemetery plots reflect the varied immigrant communities of a coal town founded in 1886.
evidence.quote: The Roslyn Cemetery is composed of 26 separate but adjacent cemetery plots, reflecting the diversity of early immigrant society.

evidence.claim: Roslyn’s 26 adjoining cemetery plots reflect the varied immigrant communities of a coal town founded in 1886.
evidence.quote: The town was founded in 1886 as a coal mining company town.

evidence.claim: Its mines supplied coal for Northern Pacific railway construction and continued railroad operations.
evidence.quote: Roslyn, which lies on the route to Stampede Pass, provided the coal for the railway construction work as well as the continuing railroad operations.

evidence.claim: Workers came from Italy, Poland, Slovakia and other European countries.
evidence.quote: Between 1886 and 1929, immigrant workers from countries such as Italy, Poland, Slovakia

evidence.claim: As diesel replaced coal-fired steam trains, mining became unprofitable; the last local mine closed in 1963.
evidence.quote: As coal-fired steam trains were being replaced by diesel power, the last mine in the area closed in 1963 as business became unprofitable.

evidence.claim: Buildings from the coal years remain, including the Northwestern Improvement Company Store at First Street and Pennsylvania Avenue.
evidence.quote: the Northwestern Improvement Company Store, now listed on the National Register of Historic Places; it still stands at the corner of First Street and Pennsylvania Avenue.

evidence.claim: Later, Roslyn and its surroundings supplied the exterior scenes of fictional Cicely, Alaska, for Northern Exposure.
evidence.quote: Northern Exposure, a hit CBS television series, filmed its exterior scenes for the fictional town of Cicely, Alaska, in Roslyn and the surrounding area.

evidence.claim: The name Cle Elum began on a railroad depot as Clealum in 1886, drawn from the Kittitas name Tle-el-Lum, meaning “swift water.”
evidence.quote: In the spring of 1886, Northern Pacific Railway surveyors Virgil Bogue and Herbert Huson were making their way through the region with the intent of establishing a station. At the site of the future city, a depot was named Clealum after the Kittitas name Tle-el-Lum (tlielləm), meaning "swift water", referring to the Cle Elum River.

evidence.claim: The spelling became two words in 1908.
evidence.quote: In 1908, Clealum was altered to Cle Elum.

evidence.claim: A decade later, fire destroyed 29 city blocks, including 30 businesses and 205 houses.
evidence.quote: on June 25, 1918, when a huge fire wiped out over seventy acres of the city (29 city blocks)

evidence.claim: A decade later, fire destroyed 29 city blocks, including 30 businesses and 205 houses.
evidence.quote: Thirty businesses and 205 houses were destroyed

evidence.claim: The 1906 Cle Elum State Bank Building survived.
evidence.quote: One of the few buildings in downtown Cle Elum to survive the fire was the Cle Elum State Bank Building, built in 1906; it still stands today.

evidence.claim: Downtown was quickly rebuilt in brick, and many of those buildings remain.
evidence.quote: The rest of downtown was quickly rebuilt with brick and many of these buildings still stand.

evidence.claim: The bank and the rebuilt streetscape mark two different chapters in the town’s surviving architecture.
evidence.quote: One of the few buildings in downtown Cle Elum to survive the fire was the Cle Elum State Bank Building, built in 1906; it still stands today. The rest of downtown was quickly rebuilt with brick and many of these buildings still stand.

evidence.claim: Thorp Mill retains handmade wooden machinery from a business that milled flour for Kittitas Valley residents from 1883 until 1946.
evidence.quote: showcases a remarkable collection of handmade wooden mill machinery. Constructed in 1883, it served as an essential place for flour milling and social interaction for Kittitas County residents until 1946.

evidence.claim: Farmers brought wheat by wagon to be ground into flour, bran or livestock feed.
evidence.quote: Kittitas Valley farmers brought their wheat crops to the Thorp Mill in wagons, and the grain was ground into flour, bran, or feed for livestock.

evidence.claim: The first grinding stones came by wagon from The Dalles, Oregon.
evidence.quote: Initially the grain was processed between huge stone burrs that had been brought laboriously via wagon from The Dalles, Oregon.

evidence.claim: When the Northern Pacific depot arrived in 1895, the railway enabled the installation of more efficient steel rollers and gave farmers a route to Puget Sound markets.
evidence.quote: In 1895, the arrival of the Northern Pacific Railroad depot enabled importation and installation of more efficient steel roller burrs. The railroad also provided local farmers with an easy means to sell their flour throughout the Puget Sound region.

evidence.claim: Look for the collection of handmade wooden mill machinery.
evidence.quote: showcases a remarkable collection of handmade wooden mill machinery.

evidence.claim: Near Thorp, the high forests of the Cascade Range give way to fields growing timothy hay and alfalfa, a change from the coal towns farther up the corridor.
evidence.quote: where high elevation forests of the Cascade Range give way to cattle ranches surrounded by farmlands noted for timothy hay, alfalfa, vegetables, and fruit production.

evidence.claim: The river behind the town’s name meets the Yakima River near the town.
evidence.quote: The town takes its name from the Cle Elum River, which meets the Yakima River near here.

evidence.claim: Water diverted from the Yakima through canals powered a horizontal wheel shared by the gristmill and a neighboring sawmill.
evidence.quote: The mill utilized Yakima River water brought to the area through a system of canals. A horizontal water wheel powered both the gristmill and a nearby sawmill.
